a: touches pitch
p: Ben Sira opens his warning about the rich with an image from daily life: tar does not wash off.
b: Pitch (Greek pissa) is the black, sticky tar of pine resin or bitumen used to seal boats and jars. You cannot handle it and stay clean. The Hebrew of Cairo Genizah manuscript A (folio V recto, lines 21-22) says it even more bluntly: "whoever touches pitch, his hand sticks" and "whoever joins a scoffer learns his way." The point is not that the rich are evil in themselves (13:24 says wealth can be good) but that close partnership with the proud powerful slowly makes you like them. Paul quotes a Greek proverb with the same idea: "bad company ruins good habits" (1 Corinthians 15:33).
orig: Ὁ ἁπτόμενος πίσσης μολυνθήσεται (ho haptomenos pissēs molynthēsetai), "the one touching pitch will be stained"

a: What do a cooking pot and a metal cauldron have in common?
t: The clay pot and the cauldron
p: A partnership of the weak and the strong is like an earthenware pot knocking against a metal one.
b: The Greek chytra is an ordinary earthenware cooking pot; a lebēs is a large metal cauldron or kettle. Put them in the same tub and the cauldron is not hurt; the pot cracks. Ben Sira is not talking about friendship in general but about business partnership and alliance with "someone stronger and richer" (the same verb koinōneō, "share, be partners," runs through 13:1, 2 and 17). The Hebrew of manuscript A adds a third line that spells the picture out (folio V recto, line 25): "or how can a rich man be joined to a poor one?"

a: snorts with anger
p: The Greek verb is the one used of Jesus' deep anger or sternness in Mark and John.
b: The rich man "does wrong, and he himself" prosenebrimēsato, a strong word for snorting with rage. Its simple form embrimaomai is the verb the Gospels use when Jesus speaks sternly to the man he healed (Mark 1:43) and when anger stirs in him at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:33, 38). Here the anger is the injustice: the man who did the wrong acts offended, and the one wronged must apologize. The Hebrew of manuscript A differs in its wording but makes the same contrast: the poor man who was wronged is the one who "pleads for favor" (yitchanan, folio V recto, line 26). The Greek says only that he "will beg besides."

a: wag his head at you
p: A gesture of scorn in the Bible, used of passers-by at Jerusalem's fall and at the cross.
b: Moving the head at someone is mockery. The psalmist's enemies "shake their heads" (Psalm 22:7); passers-by "wag their heads at Daughter Jerusalem" (Lamentations 2:15); and at the cross "they shook their heads" (Matthew 27:39). Ben Sira draws the whole scene of 13:4-7 from the life of a client who tries to keep up with a rich patron: the free dinners are a trap, the patron drains him "twice or three times," then laughs at the man he has ruined. A first reader in Jerusalem's small upper class about 190-180 BC would have seen this happen.

a: When a powerful man invites you, hold back
t: Hold back, and be invited again
p: The same table manners as Proverbs 25 and Jesus' parable of the places at a wedding.
b: Ben Sira gives practical advice for dealing with a dynastēs, a man of power: do not rush in (13:10), do not stay away, do not act as an equal (13:11). Proverbs already taught, "It is better for him to say to you, 'Come up here'" (Proverbs 25:7), and Jesus tells guests to take the last place, "so that when the man who invited you comes, he will tell you, 'Friend, come up higher'" (Luke 14:10). Jesus turns the advice into a picture of the kingdom: "everyone who raises himself up will be brought low" (Luke 14:11). Ben Sira stays at the level of good sense in a world of patrons.

a: keep your words to himself
t: A man who cannot keep a secret
p: The Greek line is hard; the Hebrew of manuscript A has a different picture of a cruel man who sets up a ruler and plots against many.
b: The Greek says, word for word, "merciless is the one not keeping words." Most readers take it as "the one who does not keep your words (secret)": the powerful man will use what you told him against you, with beatings and chains. The Hebrew of Genizah manuscript A (folio V verso, lines 6-7) reads differently: akhzari yitten moshel, "a cruel man will set up a ruler (or: dominion), and he does not pity; against the lives of many he ties a plot." Hart (1909) renders the first words "he that is cruel will establish dominion." Kahana's edition (1912) prints kos'hel, "a stumbling block," in place of the manuscript's moshel. Both versions warn the same young man: the great man's friendly talk (13:11) is an interrogation.
orig: ἀνελεήμων ὁ μὴ συντηρῶν λόγους (anelēēmōn ho mē syntērōn logous); Hebrew אכזרי יתן מושל (MS A, folio V verso, line 6)

a: Every living thing loves what is like it
t: Quoted in the Talmud "in the Writings"
p: The Babylonian Talmud quotes a form of this saying as if it stood among the Writings of Scripture.
b: In the Babylonian Talmud (Bava Kamma 92b) Rava asks where a popular proverb comes from, and Rabba bar Mari answers that the matter is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets and stated a third time in the Writings, citing for the Writings: "Every bird nests with its kind, and a human being with one like him." That is a form of 13:15-16, though not the wording of the Hebrew of manuscript A, which says "all flesh loves its kind" (folio V verso, line 8). The rabbis did not count Ben Sira as Scripture: in Sanhedrin 100b Rav Yosef says it is forbidden to read the book, though in the same passage he goes on to say that its good sayings may be taught even in public. Yet here a line of his is introduced as "written" and placed in the third part of the Hebrew Bible. The Talmud does not name him.

a: What can a wolf share with a lamb?
p: The pairing is the prophets' picture of a world made new, and Paul's question about mismatched partners.
b: Isaiah pictures the age to come as the time when "the wolf will stay as a guest with the lamb" (Isaiah 11:6; compare Isaiah 65:25). Ben Sira speaks of this age: here the wolf eats the lamb, and a sinner cannot be a real partner of the godly, any more than a hyena can live at peace with a dog (13:18). Paul asks the same kind of questions: "What share do righteousness and lawlessness have? Or what does light have in common with darkness?" (2 Corinthians 6:14). Jesus sends his disciples out "like sheep into the middle of a pack of wolves" (Matthew 10:16).

a: hyena
p: Striped hyenas lived in the land; the Hebrew word is tsavua.
b: The Greek hyaina and the Hebrew of manuscript A, tsavua (folio V verso, line 11), both name the striped hyena, a scavenger of the Judean hills that would raid flocks and clash with the shepherds' dogs. The hyena and the dog are natural enemies, as the rich and the needy are in Ben Sira's world: the next verse makes the poor the "pasture" of the rich.

a: Wild donkeys in the desert are what lions hunt
p: Job also pictures the poor as wild donkeys scraping for food in the wilderness.
b: The wild donkey (onager) roamed the steppe and the desert edge and was a lion's natural prey. Job uses the same animal for the hungry poor who must search for food: "Look: wild donkeys in the wilderness, / out at their work, scouring for food" (Job 24:5). Ben Sira sharpens it: the poor are the nomai, the "grazing grounds," of the rich. The prophets made the same charge against the powerful who "grind the faces of the poor" (Isaiah 3:15; Amos 2:6-7).

a: he speaks good sense, and no one gives him room
p: Proverbs and Ecclesiastes noticed the same thing: wealth buys friends and a hearing.
b: Ben Sira paints in detail what Proverbs states in short sayings: "Wealth brings in friend after friend, / but a poor man gets cut off from the friend he has" (Proverbs 19:4; compare Proverbs 14:20; Proverbs 19:7). Ecclesiastes tells of a poor wise man who saved a town, yet "a poor man's wisdom is looked down on, and no one listens to his words" (Ecclesiastes 9:16). James warns a church against the same favoritism toward the man in fine clothes (James 2:1-7). Ben Sira describes; he does not here condemn. His advice is to know how the world works.

a: they declare him in the right
p: The Greek is the verb "justify," used here of a crowd excusing a rich man's bad words.
b: The Greek edikaiōsan auton is literally "they justified him": they declared him in the right. In the Law, judges are to "declare the one in the right to be in the right" (Deuteronomy 25:1); Isaiah condemns those "who for a bribe say the wicked are in the right" (Isaiah 5:23). Ben Sira shows the same corruption in ordinary social life. Paul's great word for God declaring sinners righteous is the same verb, used in a very different setting.

a: Wealth is good if there is no sin in it
p: Ben Sira says riches can be good; the New Testament warns more sharply. Both are in the churches' Bibles.
b: Ben Sira is no enemy of wealth: it is good "if there is no sin in it," and he gives rules for using it (14:11-16). This agrees with Proverbs, where wealth is often a blessing (Proverbs 10:22). The New Testament keeps that balance but presses harder on the danger: "People who are set on getting rich fall into temptation" (1 Timothy 6:9), and Jesus says it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom (Mark 10:23-25). Where Ben Sira stresses that the rich wrong the poor (13:3-7, 19-23), James and Luke say the same (James 5:1-6; Luke 6:24). So here the book agrees with the 66 books rather than going beyond them.

a: working out proverbs takes hard thinking
p: A teacher of proverbs admits his craft is labor. Ecclesiastes says much study wears out the flesh.
b: Ben Sira was a scribe whose work was finding and shaping sayings (39:1-3; 50:27). Here he admits it: "finding proverbs" means "reasonings with toil." Ecclesiastes ends on a similar note: "much study wears out the flesh" (Ecclesiastes 12:12). The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio V verso, line 20) reads "withdrawal and musing are a thought of toil," and the first half of the verse ties it together: a man's face shows what his heart is doing (13:25), so the thinker looks worn and the happy man bright (compare Ecclesiastes 8:1, "Wisdom lights up a person's face").

a: has not slipped with his mouth
p: A blessing on the one who never trips in speech; James says the same of the "complete man."
b: The "happy" sayings (Greek makarios, Hebrew ashre) of 14:1-2 begin a short section on the inner life before the long warning against the miser. Ben Sira often warns about the dangers of speech (5:13; 19:16; 28:12-26). James writes, "Whoever never trips in what he says is a complete man, able to bridle the whole body as well" (James 3:2). The second line, "stung with grief over sin," pictures the sharp pain of a guilty conscience; the next verse speaks of the soul that does not condemn its owner.

a: whose own soul does not condemn him
p: Ben Sira and John both speak of the heart or soul that does not accuse a person before God.
b: The Greek ou kategnō hē psychē autou means "his soul did not condemn him." The New Testament has the same thought: "Beloved, if our heart does not accuse us, we have freedom to speak with God" (1 John 3:21). Neither verse claims a person is sinless; both describe the peace of someone who lives honestly before God. The second line in the longer Greek (minuscules 106, 248, 253) adds "his hope in the Lord," which the KJV follows.
orig: οὐ κατέγνω ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ (ou kategnō hē psychē autou)

a: a grudging man
p: Greek baskanos and Hebrew ra' ayin: the stingy, envious look that Proverbs and Jesus warn against.
b: Greek baskanos means envious or stingy, and it carries an old folk belief about the "evil eye" that can harm by a look. The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio V verso, line 23) has ish ra' ayin, "a man with a bad eye," the same phrase Proverbs uses: "Do not take a meal from a man with a grudging eye" (Proverbs 23:6; compare Proverbs 28:22). In the Bible the "evil eye" is a heart that begrudges others, not magic. Jesus uses it so: "Or is your eye evil because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15; compare Matthew 6:23). Ben Sira's portrait in 14:3-10 is of a man so mean that he will not even spend on himself.
orig: ἀνθρώπῳ βασκάνῳ (anthrōpō baskanō); Hebrew ולאיש רע עין (ul'ish ra' ayin)

a: Whoever hoards by denying himself hoards for others
p: Ecclesiastes asked the same bitter question: for whom am I toiling and keeping myself from good things?
b: Ecclesiastes describes a man with no son or brother whose "eye never has its fill of riches," who finally asks, "For whom am I toiling ... and keeping myself from good things?" (Ecclesiastes 4:8; compare Ecclesiastes 2:18-19). A psalm says a man "heaps things up, not knowing who will haul them in" (Psalm 39:6). In Jesus' parable, God says to the rich man, "what you have made ready, who will get it?" (Luke 12:20). Ben Sira draws a practical lesson from the same fact: use what you have, on yourself, on friends and for God (14:11-16).

a: A greedy man's eye is never filled by his share
t: The eye that is never full
p: Proverbs and Ecclesiastes use the same image of an eye that never has enough.
b: "Sheol and Abaddon never have enough, / and the eyes of humans never have enough" (Proverbs 27:20); "No eye has its fill of seeing" (Ecclesiastes 1:8). The Greek pleonektēs, "greedy man," is the word family the New Testament uses for greed (Luke 12:15; Colossians 3:5). The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio V verso, lines 26-27) is different and harder: "In the eye of the stumbling man his portion is small, and he who takes his neighbor's portion destroys his own."

a: My child
p: Ben Sira speaks as a teacher to a student. The Greek says "child"; the Hebrew here says "my son."
b: The Greek teknon is "child" and can include a daughter, so the Plain says "my child." But the Hebrew of manuscript A at this verse (folio V verso, line 29) has beni, "my son," the address of Proverbs (Proverbs 1:8; Proverbs 3:11), and the book's first audience was young men in a teacher's school (51:23). Ben Sira's advice about wives, business, and the courts of the powerful assumes a male student. Readers ever since, men and women, have heard it as addressed to them.

a: the covenant of Hades
p: Hades is the Greek name for Sheol, the world of the dead. Its "covenant" is the fixed rule that all die.
b: Hades is the word the Greek Bible uses for Hebrew Sheol, the shadowy world of the dead where all go, good and bad (Psalm 6:5; Ecclesiastes 9:10). The Plain keeps "Hades," as in Revelation. The phrase diathēkē hadou, "covenant of Hades," translates a Hebrew phrase that manuscript A (folio VI recto, line 2) gives as choq lish'ol, "a decree for Sheol": the appointed rule that every person must die. "No one has shown you" it means no one knows his own hour. Isaiah mocks rulers who boast, "We have cut a covenant with death; / with Sheol we have signed a pact" (Isaiah 28:15).
orig: διαθήκη ᾅδου (diathēkē hadou); Hebrew וחוק לשאול (vechoq lish'ol)

a: for no one goes looking for luxury in Hades
t: Enjoy life, for there is nothing after?
p: Ben Sira expects no joys after death. The New Testament hope of resurrection goes beyond him.
b: Ben Sira's reason for enjoying what you have is that Hades holds no pleasure. Ecclesiastes says almost the same: "there is no doing and no reckoning, no knowledge and no wisdom in Sheol" (Ecclesiastes 9:10; compare Ecclesiastes 5:18-19). Nowhere in chapters 13-18 does Ben Sira speak of a life after death (see 17:27-28). Paul quotes the slogan "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" as the logic of a life with no resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:32), and Jesus' rich fool plans to "eat, drink, celebrate" just before his death (Luke 12:19-20). Ben Sira's advice is gentler than either: give to friends, honor God, share (14:11-13). But on the hope beyond death, the New Testament teaching on resurrection plainly goes beyond him, and churches that read him as Scripture read this line in the light of that later teaching.

a: "You will die, yes die."
p: Ben Sira quotes God's warning in Eden, in the Septuagint's own words.
b: "You will die, yes die" is the site's Plain for God's warning about the tree in Genesis 2:17, where Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament made before Jesus, renders it thanatō apothaneisthe, and Ben Sira's grandson uses the same form, thanatō apothanē. So "the covenant of ages past" is the sentence on Adam, which now binds "all flesh." The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI recto, line 7) says, "the decree of old: they will surely perish." Ben Sira treats death as the natural lot of mortals, a law of creation (17:1-2; 41:3-4); he does not here connect it with a fall, as Paul later does (Romans 5:12).
orig: Θανάτῳ ἀποθανῇ (thanatō apothanē); Hebrew וחוק עולם גוע יגועו

a: wears out like a garment
p: The psalmist says the heavens and earth will wear out like a coat; Ben Sira says it of every living body.
b: "All of them will wear thin like a coat; / you will change them like clothing" (Psalm 102:26), quoted in Hebrews 1:11. Isaiah says his accusers "will fall apart like old clothes" (Isaiah 50:9). Ben Sira applies the image to all flesh: bodies wear out as surely as cloth.

a: Like leaves thriving on a thick tree
p: Homer's Iliad compares human generations to leaves. A borrowing is possible but not provable.
b: In Homer's Iliad (6.146-149) a warrior says that the generations of men are like the generations of leaves: the wind scatters some on the ground, the forest puts out others in spring, and so one generation of men springs up and another passes away. Ben Sira's picture is very close: leaves fall and grow, "one comes to its end, and another is born." Jerusalem in the 180s BC was ruled by Greek kings, so a borrowing is possible. But the image is natural to anyone who watches trees, and the Bible has its own forms of it: "All flesh is grass" (Isaiah 40:6); "We wither like a leaf, all of us" (Isaiah 64:6). Verdict: a real parallel; borrowing is possible but not provable.

a: whose thoughts dwell on Wisdom
t: Happy is the one who meditates
p: The Hebrew verb is the one in Psalm 1:2: the happy man "murmurs over" God's law.
b: This new blessing begins a love poem about seeking Wisdom (14:20-15:10), and its first word, "Happy," with the Hebrew verb yehgeh of manuscript A (folio VI recto, line 9), "he murmurs, meditates," recalls Psalm 1: "Happy is the person ... the law of the LORD is his delight, / and he murmurs over his law day and night" (Psalm 1:1-2). In Psalm 1 the object is the Law; here it is Wisdom. Ben Sira will soon say they are one: whoever "has a firm hold on the law will win her" (15:1; compare 24:23).

a: like a tracker
p: The student is pictured as a hunter, then a lover at her window, then a guest who camps by her house.
b: In 14:22-27 the seeker of Wisdom moves closer step by step: he tracks her like game, lies in wait at her doors, peeks through her windows, camps by her walls, pitches his tent beside her, sets his children in her shade. The window scene echoes the lover of the Song of Songs, "looking in through the windows" (Song of Songs 2:9), and Proverbs' Wisdom says, "Happy is the person who listens to me, / staying awake at my doors day after day" (Proverbs 8:34). The next verses complete the picture: Wisdom comes out to meet him as a mother and a bride (15:2). Wisdom of Solomon later says, "I wanted to bring her home as my bride" (Wisdom of Solomon 8:2).
r: Song of Songs 2:9; Proverbs 8:34; Proverbs 4:6-8; Wisdom of Solomon 8:2; 15:2; 51:13-21

a: He will put his children in her shade
p: Wisdom becomes a tree; the Hebrew says the seeker "sets his nest in her leaves."
b: Now Wisdom is a great tree. The Greek skepē means shelter or shade; the Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI recto, lines 13-14) says, "he sets his nest in her foliage, and lodges among her branches." The picture of birds nesting in a tree's branches is used of kingdoms in Ezekiel 31:6 and Daniel 4:12, and of the kingdom of God in Jesus' parable of the mustard seed (Matthew 13:32). In chapter 24 Wisdom compares herself to a cedar, a palm and a vine (24:13-17).
orig: ἐν τῇ σκέπῃ αὐτῆς; Hebrew וישים קנו בעֳופיה

a: has a firm hold on the law
p: Whoever fears the Lord and holds the law will win Wisdom. Ben Sira makes the two belong together.
b: The Greek ho enkratēs tou nomou is "the one who has mastery of the law"; the Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI recto, line 15) has "the one who grasps Torah." The "this" that the God-fearer will do is the courting of Wisdom just described (14:20-27). For Ben Sira the fear of the Lord, keeping the Law of Moses, and gaining Wisdom are one path, not three (1:26; 19:20). In chapter 24 he says outright that all Wisdom's praise is "the book of the covenant of God Most High, / the law Moses commanded" (24:23).
orig: ὁ ἐγκρατὴς τοῦ νόμου (ho enkratēs tou nomou); Hebrew ותופש תורה

a: like a mother
p: Wisdom meets her seeker as a mother and welcomes him as the wife of his youth.
b: The pursuit of 14:20-27 ends with a homecoming. Wisdom meets the seeker like a mother and receives him like the woman he married when young (Greek gynē parthenias, "wife of virginity"; Hebrew eshet ne'urim in manuscript A, folio VI recto, line 16, "wife of youth," as in Proverbs 5:18 and Malachi 2:14). Proverbs already calls Wisdom a woman to love and embrace (Proverbs 4:6-8; Proverbs 7:4), and Wisdom of Solomon says, "I wanted to bring her home as my bride" (Wisdom of Solomon 8:2). Christian writers later read such passages of Christ, the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Those readings belong especially to chapter 24.
orig: ὡς γυνὴ παρθενείας; Hebrew וכאשת נעורים
r: Proverbs 5:18; Proverbs 4:6-8; Proverbs 7:4; Malachi 2:14; Wisdom of Solomon 8:2; 1 Corinthians 1:24; 24:1-22

a: bread of understanding
p: Wisdom feeds and gives drink, as in Proverbs 9; Christians heard an echo in Jesus' bread and water of life.
b: In Proverbs, Wisdom calls, "Come, have some of my bread, / and drink the wine I mixed" (Proverbs 9:5), and Isaiah invites the thirsty to "come to the water" (Isaiah 55:1). In Ben Sira, Wisdom later says that those who eat and drink her will still hunger and thirst for more (24:21). Jesus speaks of himself in the same terms: "I am the bread of life. Anyone coming to me will not go hungry at all, and the one who believes in me will not thirst again, not ever" (John 6:35; compare John 4:14). John's Gospel gives Jesus the role that Proverbs and Ben Sira give Wisdom: the host who feeds and satisfies.

a: Praise does not look right in a sinner's mouth
p: A psalm says God rebukes the wicked who recite his covenant; Ben Sira says praise must come with wisdom.
b: "But God says to the wicked: / 'What business do you have listing my rules / and carrying my covenant in your mouth?'" (Psalm 50:16). Ben Sira says the sinner's praise was "not sent by the Lord": real praise is a gift of God that grows out of wisdom (15:10). Behind both lies the prophets' charge that worship without obedience is empty (Isaiah 1:11-17; Amos 5:21-24).

a: Do not say
t: "Do not say": Ben Sira answers an excuse
p: Ben Sira quotes the excuses of people who blame God for their sins, and answers them. James does the same.
b: "Do not say" is Ben Sira's way of answering an opinion he wants to refute (5:1-6; 16:17; 11:23-24). Here the opinion is that God caused my sin: "The Lord is the reason I turned away," "He himself sent me off course." The answer comes in three steps: God hates sin (15:11-13); he made humans free to choose (15:14-17); he sees everything and never ordered anyone to sin (15:18-20). The same excuse and the same answer appear in James: "When someone is being tempted, he must never say, 'It is God who is tempting me.' God is beyond the reach of evil's temptation, and he tempts no one himself" (James 1:13). The likeness is close: the same excuse, the same refusal, and in both the person's own desire as the real source (James 1:14; 15:14-15).

a: the hand of his own choice
p: Greek diaboulion is one's own deliberation. The Hebrew has yetser, the "inclination" of later Jewish teaching.
b: "Hand" means power or control: God left the human being "in the hand of" his own diaboulion, his power to deliberate and decide. The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI recto, line 25) has yitsro, "his yetser," from the verb "to shape, form." In Genesis the yetser of the human heart is "evil from youth on" (Genesis 8:21; compare Genesis 6:5, the site's "every plan their hearts shaped"). For Ben Sira the yetser is not a demon or an evil nature but the capacity to choose, which can go either way. The rabbis later spoke of two inclinations, the good and the evil: the Mishnah reads "love the LORD your God with all your heart" as "with both your inclinations" (Mishnah Berakhot 9:5), and the Talmud has God say, "I created an evil inclination ... and I created Torah as its antidote" (Kiddushin 30b).
orig: ἐν χειρὶ διαβουλίου αὐτοῦ (en cheiri diabouliou autou); Hebrew ביד יצרו (beyad yitsro)
r: Genesis 6:5; Genesis 8:21; Deuteronomy 30:15-19; 17:6; Mishnah Berakhot 9:5; Kiddushin 30b

a: He has set fire and water before you
t: Fire and water, life and death
p: Ben Sira retells Moses' "choose life" (Deuteronomy 30) with a picture of two opposite elements.
b: Moses said, "See, today I am placing before you life and what is good, death and what is bad," and, "Life and death are what I have put before you, blessing and curse. Choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:15, 19). Ben Sira's "Life and death lie in front of people" (15:17) echoes the Greek of Deuteronomy 30:15, which has the same nouns. "Fire and water" add a picture: two things that cannot be mixed, set side by side so that you must reach for one. Jeremiah made the same offer to his city, "the way of life and the way of death" (Jeremiah 21:8). Jesus' two gates and two roads (Matthew 7:13-14) set out the same choice.

a: what each one is pleased to choose will be given to him
p: Ben Sira agrees with Moses that people can choose. Paul says more about why they fail.
b: Ben Sira's teaching agrees with the call of Deuteronomy 30 and the prophets' pleas to "turn back" (Ezekiel 18:31-32). It goes no further than they do. Paul adds what Ben Sira does not discuss: the power of sin in the person who wants the good, "The good that I want, I do not do" (Romans 7:19), and that salvation "is not up to the one who wills ... but to God, who shows mercy" (Romans 9:16). Ben Sira himself does not deny God's mercy (16:11-12; 17:29). What kind of freedom 15:14 speaks of is the point on which churches have read the verse differently; see the card on this chapter, and the card at Deuteronomy 30 on whether fallen people can choose to turn to God.

a: His eyes are on those who fear him
p: A line close to Psalm 33:18, with the next clause turning it into a warning: he sees every deed.
b: "Look: the LORD's eye is toward those who fear him" (Psalm 33:18; compare Psalm 34:15). In the psalms this is comfort. Ben Sira uses it in an argument: the Lord who sees everything (15:18) also "takes note of every work of man," so no sinner can claim that God made him sin without knowing it. "In every place the LORD has his eyes open, / on the lookout over evil people and good" (Proverbs 15:3).

a: He gave no one an order to be ungodly
t: Is God the author of sin?
p: Ben Sira's answer is no. Orthodox teaching and the Mishnah agree, each in its own way.
b: Ben Sira ends by denying that God ever commands or permits sin. The Orthodox Confession of Dositheus (1672) says "God is in no way the author of evil" (Decree 4). Jewish teaching held God's knowledge and human freedom together: "Everything is foreseen yet freedom of choice is granted" (Mishnah Avot 3:15). Josephus, writing in the late first century AD, says that in the time of Jonathan the high priest, a few decades after Ben Sira, the Jewish parties divided on this question: the Essenes said fate governs all things, the Sadducees that "all our actions are in our own power," and the Pharisees that some things are the work of fate and some in our own power (Antiquities 13.171-173). Ben Sira does not use the language of fate, and he stresses human choice (15:14-17).

a: many children who are no good
p: In a world that counted many children a blessing, Ben Sira ranks godliness higher. Wisdom of Solomon agrees.
b: In Israel, children were the gift of God (Psalm 127:3-5) and childlessness a grief (1 Samuel 1:5-11). Ben Sira does not deny that, but he puts the fear of the Lord first: many children without it are no cause for joy, and "it is better to die with no children than to have ungodly ones" (16:3). The Hebrew of manuscript A adds (folio VI verso, line 5), "for they will have no good end." Wisdom of Solomon says the same in Greek: "It is better to have no children and have virtue" (Wisdom of Solomon 4:1). This agrees with the 66 books rather than going beyond them: Isaiah promises the faithful eunuch "a marker and a name / that is better than sons and daughters" (Isaiah 56:5), and Jesus puts loyalty to him above family (Matthew 10:37).
r: Psalm 127:3-5; 1 Samuel 1:5-11; Wisdom of Solomon 4:1; Isaiah 56:4-5; Matthew 10:37

a: One man with understanding can fill a city with people
t: One wise man and a whole city
p: One wise person can build up a city; the Hebrew says "one childless man who fears the LORD."
b: The Greek speaks of one synetos, a person of understanding. The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI verso, line 7) ties the line to the verse before: "From one childless man who fears the LORD a city will be settled." Abraham bargained for Sodom down to ten righteous people (Genesis 18:32), and Ecclesiastes tells of a poor wise man who saved a town by his wisdom (Ecclesiastes 9:15). The lawless "tribe" of the second line will end in ruin, as the examples of 16:6-10 will show.
orig: Hebrew מאחד ערירי ירא ייי תשב עיר

a: Fire will be lit among a crowd of sinners
p: Ben Sira begins a list of judgments in the past, starting with fire like the fire that took Korah's company.
b: The "crowd" (Greek synagōgē, "gathering") of sinners who were burned is most likely Korah's company in the wilderness: "fire came out from the LORD and ate up the two hundred fifty men" (Numbers 16:35), which a psalm recalls: "A fire was lit in their community; / flames ate up the wicked" (Psalm 106:18). The list that follows (16:7-10) runs through the giants, Sodom, the Canaanites and the wilderness generation, to prove that God does not let the stubborn go unpunished (16:11).

a: He did not forgive
p: The Greek verb is the one for making atonement; with God as the one who acts, the Plain says "forgive," as the Hebrew does.
b: The Greek verb here is exilaskomai, and its noun exilasmos comes back four times in these chapters (16:11; 17:29; 18:12; 18:20). It is the word of the Day of Atonement in the Greek of Leviticus: "atonement will be made for you" (Leviticus 16:30). Where a person is the one acting, the Plain of Sirach says "atone" (3:3; 3:30). In these five verses God is the one acting, and the Plain says "forgive" and "forgiveness." The Hebrew of manuscript A supports that: here it has lo nasa, "he did not forgive" (literally "did not lift," that is, did not take the guilt away; folio VI verso, line 10), and at 16:11 "he forgives and pardons" (line 14). The Latin turns this verse around: "The ancient giants did not obtain pardon for their sins" (Douay 16:8).
orig: οὐκ ἐξιλάσατο (ouk exilasato); Hebrew אשר לא נשא

a: the giants of long ago
p: The Greek "giants" is the Septuagint's word for the mighty men of Genesis 6:4. Other Jewish books tell the same story.
b: Genesis says, "In those days the Nephilim were on the earth ... They were the heroes of ancient times" (Genesis 6:4). The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, calls them hoi gigantes hoi ap' aiōnos, "the giants of old," and Ben Sira's grandson writes tōn archaiōn gigantōn. Later Jewish books made the giants examples of pride punished: "the proud giants were dying" at the flood (Wisdom of Solomon 14:6); "Giants were among them, sure of their own strength and daring" (3 Maccabees 2:4); they "died out through their own bad counsel" (Baruch 3:28). 1 Enoch tells the longest form of the story, of Watchers whose sons were giants. Ben Sira says only that they "broke away" in their strength, and that God did not forgive them (see the next note). The Hebrew of manuscript A has "the princes of old" instead (see the variant).
r: Genesis 6:4; Wisdom of Solomon 14:6; 3 Maccabees 2:4; Baruch 3:26-28; 1 Enoch 7:2; 2 Peter 2:4-5

a: the place where Lot lived as a stranger
p: Ben Sira names pride as Sodom's sin, as Ezekiel does.
b: The Greek paroikia is a place where one lives as an outsider; Lot was a resident foreigner in Sodom (Genesis 19:9). Ben Sira does not name Sodom; he says God abhorred its people "because of their pride." Ezekiel had said the same: "Here is the guilt of Sodom ... pride, a full belly of food, and easy, quiet comfort ... But she did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy" (Ezekiel 16:49). 3 Maccabees also says, "The Sodomites practiced arrogance" (3 Maccabees 2:5). 2 Peter and Jude use the same city as a warning example (2 Peter 2:6; Jude 7).

a: the nation marked for destruction
p: The peoples of Canaan, whom the Law put "under the ban." The Hebrew says "the nation of the herem."
b: The Greek ethnos apōleias, "nation of destruction," stands for Hebrew goy cherem, "the nation of the ban" in manuscript A (folio VI verso, line 12): the peoples of Canaan whom Israel was told to "put them under the ban completely" (Deuteronomy 7:2; compare Deuteronomy 20:17). A later corrector of Codex Sinaiticus writes "Canaan" here, according to Swete's notes, and adds a line of his own (see the variant). Ben Sira reads the conquest as God's judgment on their sins (compare Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 18:24-25; Wisdom of Solomon 12:3-11), not as an arbitrary war. The moral questions the ban raises are discussed on the topic page.
orig: ἔθνος ἀπωλείας; Hebrew גוי חרם (goy cherem)
r: Deuteronomy 7:2; Deuteronomy 20:17; Genesis 15:16; Leviticus 18:24-25; Wisdom of Solomon 12:3-11

a: the six hundred thousand men on foot
p: Ben Sira ends his list with Israel's own rebels: the whole army that left Egypt and died in the desert.
b: "The people I am among number six hundred thousand men on foot," Moses says (Numbers 11:21; compare Exodus 12:37). Because they refused to enter the land, God swore that "in this wilderness your dead bodies will fall" (Numbers 14:29). Ben Sira puts Israel's own ancestors in the same list as the giants and Sodom: hard hearts are punished whoever has them. Paul and Hebrews draw the same warning from the wilderness generation (1 Corinthians 10:1-11; Hebrews 3:7-19).

a: For mercy and anger are both with him
p: Ben Sira echoes the LORD's description of himself at Sinai: forgiving, yet not leaving guilt unpunished.
b: At Sinai the LORD called himself "great in loyal love and faithfulness ... forgiving guilt, rebellion and sin. Yet he will by no means leave guilt unpunished" (Exodus 34:6-7). "Stiff-necked" is the word used there of Israel (Exodus 32:9). The line "mercy and anger are both with him" repeats 5:6 word for word in the Greek. "Mighty to forgive" is dynastēs exilasmōn, "a lord of forgivenesses" (see the note on 16:7). The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI verso, lines 14-15) says, "for mercy and anger are with him; he forgives and pardons, but on the wicked he lets his anger rest." In the last clause Abegg's transcription reads yagiah, which looks like a copying slip for yaniach, "lets rest," the word Kahana's edition prints; Hart (1909) translates it "he makes his wrath to rest." Ben Sira holds both sides together: the next verse says his correction is as large as his mercy, and 17:29 and 18:11-14 dwell on his mercy.

a: he will judge a man according to his works
p: A refrain of both Testaments: God pays each person back by what he does.
b: "You pay each person back by what he does" (Psalm 62:12). Paul repeats it: "He will pay back each person according to his works" (Romans 2:6), and so does Jesus (Matthew 16:27; Revelation 22:12). Ben Sira says it twice (16:12, 14). Christians agree that God judges deeds; they differ on how this fits with salvation by grace, a question asked on the cards for Romans 2 and James 2.

a: every gift of alms
p: Greek eleēmosynē is a gift to the poor; the Hebrew has tsedaqah, "righteousness," later Hebrew's word for charity.
b: The Greek eleēmosynē, "mercy, alms," is the word Tobit uses for gifts to the poor. The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI verso, lines 16-17) has a different first line, "Everyone who does tsedaqah has a reward," and then a second line close to the Greek: "and every person, according to his deeds, will go out before him." Tsedaqah means "righteousness," but in the later Hebrew of the rabbis it became the ordinary word for charity, and Ben Sira's Greek translator already reads it that way. The Latin goes further: "every mercy will make a place for each according to the merit of his works" (Douay). Whether giving to the poor takes away sin or earns reward is asked on the card at Tobit 4.
orig: πάσῃ ἐλεημοσύνῃ ποιήσει τόπον; Hebrew כל העושה צדקה יש לו שכר

a: The Lord hardened Pharaoh
p: Only a few verses after "Do not say God made me sin," the longer text says God hardened Pharaoh.
b: This line, found in the Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI verso, lines 18-19) and in later Greek copies (see the variant), recalls Exodus: "I will make Pharaoh's heart hard, and I will heap up my signs and my wonders" (Exodus 7:3). Its point is that God's works became known "under heaven" through Pharaoh's stubbornness, the same point Paul draws: "that my name might be told through all the earth" (Romans 9:17). Readers have long asked how this fits with 15:11-20. Exodus itself says both that Pharaoh hardened his heart and that the LORD hardened it (Exodus 8:15; Exodus 9:12), and the book of Sirach, like Exodus, holds both: God rules all, and no one may blame him for his own sin.

a: he divided his light and the darkness
p: Claude's theory: a copyist may have dropped these lines because Pharaoh's hardening seemed to clash with 15:11-20.
b: This is Claude's theory. Verses 16:15-16 are in the Hebrew of manuscript A and in the longer Greek (minuscules 106 and 248), but not in Vaticanus, and Swete's notes show no such lines in Sinaiticus or Alexandrinus. The Latin Vulgate lacks them too. One possible reason for cutting just these lines is theological: a scribe who had just copied "Do not say, 'He himself sent me off course'" (15:12) may have stumbled at "The Lord hardened Pharaoh." The lines also break the flow from 16:14 to 16:17, so a simple skip of two lines is just as possible. For the Latin, Hart (1909) points to a "drastic reviser" who left out 16:15-16 and changed 16:14.

a: Do not say, "I can hide from the Lord.
p: The psalms answer the same thought: there is nowhere to go from God's face.
b: The sinner reasons that in so vast a creation one soul will not be noticed. The wicked in the psalms think the same: "God forgets. / He has turned his face away; he never looks" (Psalm 10:11; compare Psalm 94:7). The psalmist answers, "Where could I go to get away from your spirit? / Where could I run from your face?" (Psalm 139:7), and the LORD asks through Jeremiah, "Can anyone hide in secret places / so that I do not see him?" (Jeremiah 23:24). The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI verso, lines 21-22) has the sinner say, "what is my soul among all the spirits of humankind?"

a: the heavens above the heavens, which are God's
p: Solomon said the heavens above the heavens cannot contain God; here they shake when he comes.
b: "Look: the heavens, the heavens above the heavens, are not big enough for you" (1 Kings 8:27); "the sky belongs to the LORD your God, even the highest heavens" (Deuteronomy 10:14). The Greek ho ouranos tou ouranou is the Hebrew way of saying "the highest heaven." When God "visits" (Greek episkopē, his coming to inspect and judge), all of it shakes (compare Psalm 18:7; Psalm 104:32; Nahum 1:5).

a: The covenant is a long way off
p: The Hebrew puts these lines in the sinner's mouth ("if I sin, no eye sees me"); the Greek can be read either way.
b: In the Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI verso, lines 24-27), verses 16:20-22 are plainly the sinner's words, in the first person: "He will not set his heart on me ... If I sin, no eye sees me ... What righteous act, who will report it?" Then 16:23 says that only a person short on sense thinks like this. The Greek is less clear. Read one way, 16:20-21 is Ben Sira's own comment (no one thinks about God's hidden works) and 16:22 the sinner's complaint; read another way, all three verses are the sinner's. "The covenant is a long way off" then means: God's promised justice is too distant to worry about. The longer Greek and the KJV add, "and the testing of all is at the end."

a: a fool who has lost his way
p: The Greek "fool" stands for a Hebrew word Proverbs uses for the naive, easily misled young man.
b: The Greek anēr aphrōn kai planōmenos is "a senseless and wandering man." The Hebrew of manuscript A (folio VI verso, line 27) has gever poteh, from the same root as Proverbs' peti, "the naive": not a stupid person but one who is open to any influence (Proverbs 1:22; Proverbs 14:15). Ben Sira's students were exactly such young men, and the sinner's reasoning of 16:17-22 is what he wants them to see through.
orig: ἀνὴρ ἄφρων καὶ πλανώμενος; Hebrew וגבור פותה

a: instruction
p: Paideia is both teaching and correction: "instruction" here, "discipline" for God's correction in 18:13-14.
b: Paideia is the Greek word for the raising and training of a child. It can mean education (what a teacher hands on) or correction (what a father or God does to set a person right). In this part of Sirach the Plain renders it "instruction" here, where Ben Sira speaks as a teacher, and "discipline" in 18:13-14, where the Lord corrects people like a shepherd (compare Proverbs 3:11-12; Hebrews 12:5-6). The Hebrew of manuscript A has a different, bolder line here (folio VI verso, line 28): "I will pour out my spirit by weight."
orig: ἐκφαίνω ἐν σταθμῷ παιδείαν; Hebrew אביעה במשקל רוחי

a: He put his works in order for all time
p: The sun, moon and stars keep their places and never tire: a theme of the psalms, Jeremiah and 1 Enoch.
b: Ben Sira begins a hymn on creation (16:26-17:14) with the heavens. The heavenly lights never went hungry or wore out, never crowded each other, and will never refuse God's word. "He made them stand for ever and ever; / he set a rule, and it will not be broken" (Psalm 148:6); he "fixed the rules for the moon and stars" (Jeremiah 31:35). 1 Enoch opens on the same note: "See how the lights in the sky never change their paths ... and none of them breaks its command" (1 Enoch 2:1). Isaiah says of God himself, "He never tires, and he never wears out" (Isaiah 40:28). The heavens' obedience is set against human disobedience in the next chapter.

a: to the earth they go back
p: Every living creature returns to the earth, as Psalm 104 and Genesis 3 say.
b: "You gather back their breath, and they die / and go back to their dust" (Psalm 104:29). The next verse applies this to the human being made "out of earth" (17:1), as in Genesis: "you are dust, / and to dust you will go back" (Genesis 3:19). The Greek psychē, here "breath of life," is the "living being" of Genesis 2:7.

a: The Lord created a human being out of earth
t: Made from the ground, returned to it
p: Ben Sira retells Genesis 2-3: the human is shaped from earth and goes back to it.
b: "Then the LORD God shaped the man from dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7), and "you are dust, / and to dust you will go back" (Genesis 3:19). Ben Sira puts both in one line, as two parts of God's plan, not as a story of reward and punishment: the same Lord who made the human "turned him back into it again." From here to 17:14 he retells Genesis 1-3 and Sinai as one story of God's gifts to humanity. The Latin moves "he made him in his own image" up into this verse.

a: days that are counted
p: Each life has a fixed number of days, as Job and the psalms say.
b: The Greek hēmeras arithmou, "days of number," means a counted, limited span. Job asks God about the man whose "days are cut to measure" (Job 14:5), and the psalmist prays, "Teach us, then, to count our days, / so that we may bring in a wise heart" (Psalm 90:12). Yet in the same breath Ben Sira gives humans power "over what is on the earth," the rule God gave in Genesis 1:28. Mortal, yet in charge: that is his picture of humanity.

a: made them in his image
p: Ben Sira links the image of God to the strength and rule God gave humans, as Genesis 1:26-28 does.
b: "Then God said, 'Let us make humankind in our image, as our likeness. Let them rule over the fish of the sea'" (Genesis 1:26). In Genesis the image is followed at once by rule over the creatures, and Ben Sira does the same: strength, image, and the fear of humans laid on every animal (17:4). The Greek kat' eikona autou is the Septuagint's phrase in Genesis 1:27. Readers have understood the image as reason and freedom, as ruling on God's behalf, or as relationship with God; Ben Sira's list of gifts in 17:6-7 leans toward the first two. The topic page sets out the views.

a: He put the fear of them on all flesh
p: After the flood God said the fear of humans would be on every animal. Ben Sira puts it at creation.
b: "The fear and terror of you will be on every wild animal of the earth and every bird of the sky" (Genesis 9:2). In Genesis this is said to Noah after the flood; Ben Sira, folding the stories together, makes it part of the first creation. The second line, "to be masters over beasts and birds," is the rule of Genesis 1:28 and Psalm 8:6-8.

a: He gave them choice
p: The same word as 15:14: diaboulion, the power to deliberate, here listed among the gifts of creation.
b: The list starts with diaboulion, the word translated "choice" in 15:14, where the Hebrew had yetser. Here it is a gift like the tongue, the eyes and the heart: part of what it means to be human. In 15:14-17 the same gift makes people responsible for their sins. Ben Sira never treats the capacity to choose as evil in itself.

a: pointed out to them what is good and what is evil
t: Knowing good and evil: gift or forbidden fruit?
p: In Genesis, knowing good and evil is the forbidden fruit. Ben Sira calls it a gift from God.
b: Genesis has "the tree of knowing good and evil" in the garden (Genesis 2:9), forbidden to the man, and the snake promises, "you will be like God, knowing both good and evil" (Genesis 3:5). Ben Sira says God himself filled humans with knowledge and "pointed out to them what is good and what is evil," and he tells this creation story without a fall. Some readers see a real difference: Ben Sira treats moral knowledge as part of the Creator's gift, the Genesis story as something grasped against God's command. Others reconcile the two: God gave the knowledge of right and wrong that his commands assume (Deuteronomy 30:15; the Septuagint has the same words, "the good and the evil"), while the tree stood for deciding good and evil for oneself. Ben Sira speaks of where sin began elsewhere, in a much-debated line (25:24).

a: the law of life
p: Without a break, Ben Sira moves from the creation of humanity to the giving of the Law at Sinai.
b: In 17:1-10 "they" are all human beings; in 17:11-14 "they" receive "the law of life," an "everlasting covenant," see God's glory and hear his voice: this is Sinai (Exodus 19-20; Deuteronomy 5). Ben Sira does not mark the shift, as though the Law were the completion of God's gifts to humanity. He calls Moses' law "the law of life and knowledge" again in 45:5 and says Moses gave Israel the commandments "face to face." Deuteronomy says the same of the Law: "Then you will live" (Deuteronomy 30:16). Paul, by contrast, says the commandment "meant for life" turned out to bring death because of sin (Romans 7:10).

a: Their eyes saw his majestic glory
p: Israel saw God's glory and heard his voice from the fire, as Deuteronomy says.
b: "You said, 'Look, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and his greatness, and we have heard his voice out of the fire'" (Deuteronomy 5:24; compare Exodus 19:16-19). Ben Sira's two lines match Deuteronomy's pair, glory seen and voice heard. "His" voice follows Sinaiticus and Ephraemi; Vaticanus has "their" (see the variant).

a: he gave each one orders about his neighbor
p: Ben Sira sums up the Law in two parts: avoid all wrong, and do right by your neighbor.
b: "Watch out for anything unjust" and "orders about his neighbor" sum up the second half of the Ten Commandments and the law of Leviticus: "You are to love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD" (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus called this the second great commandment (Matthew 22:39), and Paul said love of neighbor fulfills the law (Romans 13:9-10).

a: For each nation he appointed a ruler
p: Each nation has a "ruler," but Israel is the Lord's own share: Ben Sira echoes Deuteronomy 32:8-9.
b: Deuteronomy says the Most High divided the nations "to match the number of the sons of God," while "the LORD's own share is his people" (Deuteronomy 32:8-9). The Septuagint of Deuteronomy 32:8 has "according to the number of the angels of God," and its 32:9 has meris Kyriou, "the Lord's portion," the same words Ben Sira uses. So the "ruler" (Greek hēgoumenos) of each nation may be an angelic prince, like "the prince of the kingdom of Persia" in Daniel (Daniel 10:13, 20), or simply its human king (compare 10:4). Either way, Israel has no go-between: God rules it directly. The longer Greek adds a fuller line (see the variant).

a: his firstborn
p: The longer text calls Israel God's firstborn, as the LORD did in Exodus.
b: "This is what the LORD says: Israel is my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22; the Septuagint, huios prōtotokos mou Israēl). Hart's minuscule 248 uses a related word, prōtogonos, and pictures God as a nurse rearing the child with discipline, as in Deuteronomy: "the LORD your God trains you the way a man trains his son" (Deuteronomy 8:5). The line is not in Vaticanus.

a: like a seal ring
t: A seal ring and the pupil of the eye
p: God keeps a person's almsgiving as close as a ring on his hand and as carefully as an eye.
b: A seal ring was a person's signature, worn always on the hand (Haggai 2:23, "I will make you like a seal ring"; compare Song of Songs 8:6). "The pupil of the eye" is what a person protects without thinking; God "guarded him like the pupil of his eye" (Deuteronomy 32:10), and the psalmist prays, "Guard me like the pupil of the eye" (Psalm 17:8). So acts of mercy are kept safe with God. The longer Greek adds, "giving repentance to his sons and daughters," which the KJV follows.
r: Haggai 2:23; Song of Songs 8:6; Deuteronomy 32:10; Psalm 17:8; 16:14

a: he will rise and repay them
p: God "rising up" is the psalms' picture of God acting as judge. Later readers also heard resurrection.
b: "So now I will get up," says the LORD in Psalm 12:5, when he acts for the poor; God "rising" is a picture of him taking his seat as judge (compare Isaiah 33:10). Ben Sira means that God, who sees all sins (17:19-20), will act and repay. The Latin, which uses the word for resurrection (resurget), adds "and he will turn them down into the depths of the earth." Hart (1909) suggests the Latin addition grew from reading "he will rise" as the resurrection; Ben Sira himself does not speak of a resurrection (17:27-28).

a: for those who repent he has opened a road back
p: Greek metanoeō, "repent," and epanodos, "a way back": the door God keeps open after judgment is announced.
b: "Repent" (Greek metanoeō) means to change one's mind and life; the Plain adds the gloss "turn your life around." Epanodos is a road home, a return trip. Right after warning of judgment (17:23), Ben Sira says God has always left a way back. Wisdom of Solomon says God looks past people's sins "to bring them to repentance" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:23), and 2 Peter says he "wants all to arrive at repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). The call that follows (17:25-26) is one of the clearest in the book.

a: Turn back to the Lord and leave your sins behind
p: Ben Sira takes up the prophets' call: turn back, and God will turn to you.
b: "Turn back, Israel, to the LORD your God" (Hosea 14:1); "Turn back to the LORD your God, / for he is gracious and compassionate" (Joel 2:13); "Return to me ... and I will return to you" (Zechariah 1:3; Malachi 3:7). Ben Sira applies the prophets' call to the individual student: leave sins, pray, and "cut down your stumbling."

a: In Hades, who will praise the Most High
p: Like several psalms, Ben Sira says the dead cannot praise God. He gives no hope of resurrection here.
b: The argument is the psalmists': turn now, because only the living can thank God. "In Sheol, who gives you thanks?" (Psalm 6:5); "The dead do not praise Yah" (Psalm 115:17); "It is not Sheol that thanks you ... The living, the living: they are the ones who thank you" (Isaiah 38:18-19). Ben Sira agrees with these books and does not go beyond them. Other books go further: Daniel 12:2 speaks of the dead waking, and 2 Maccabees, part of the Catholic and Orthodox Old Testament with Sirach, has a martyr say "the King of the world will raise us" (2 Maccabees 7:9). The New Testament proclaims resurrection in Christ (1 Corinthians 15). Churches that read Sirach as Scripture read this verse with those books, as a word about this present life.
r: Psalm 6:5; Psalm 88:10-12; Psalm 115:17; Isaiah 38:18-19; Daniel 12:2; 2 Maccabees 7:9; 1 Corinthians 15:20-22; 14:16

a: a son of man
p: Here the phrase means simply a mortal human, as in Psalm 8:4, not the title of Daniel 7 or of Jesus.
b: Greek huios anthrōpou, "son of man," is a Hebrew way of saying "a human being." "What is a mere mortal, that you remember him, / a son of man, that you look after him?" (Psalm 8:4; compare Psalm 144:3). Ben Sira's point is that humans cannot hold "everything" because they are not immortal. The phrase is the same one Jesus used of himself, with Daniel 7:13 behind it, but here it carries no such title.

a: Yet even it fails
p: The sun goes dark (in an eclipse, or each evening); how much weaker are flesh and blood.
b: The Greek ekleipei, "fails, leaves off," is the root of "eclipse." Even the brightest thing in the sky has its dark moments. The second line is hard and the copies differ: Vaticanus says "an evil man sets his mind on flesh and blood" (he thinks only of earthly things); its correctors and Alexandrinus say "flesh and blood thinks up evil," which the KJV follows (see the variant). Either way, the human mind is weaker than the sun.

a: earth and ashes
p: Abraham's words for himself before God, in the Septuagint's form "earth and ashes."
b: Abraham says, "I am only dust and ashes" (Genesis 18:27). The Septuagint there has gē kai spodos, "earth and ashes," the same pair Ben Sira uses. Job ends with the same words (Job 42:6). God watches over "the army of heaven's heights," the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19), while all humans are earth. The chapter ends where it began, with humans made of earth (17:1).

a: created all things together
p: The Greek koinē means "together, all alike." The Latin simul, "at the same time," shaped Augustine's view of creation.
b: The Greek koinē means "in common, together, all alike": the eternal God made everything there is, with nothing left out. The Latin translated it simul, "at the same time," and Augustine built on that word. In The Literal Meaning of Genesis (6.3.4; 6.6.11) he quotes "He who lives forever created all things at once" to argue that God made everything at once, so that the six days of Genesis 1 are not six stretches of ordinary time. That reading has had a long history in the debate over the days of creation. The Greek itself does not settle the timing; it stresses that nothing exists that he did not make.
orig: ἔκτισεν τὰ πάντα κοινῇ (ektisen ta panta koinē); Latin "creavit omnia simul"

a: The Lord alone will be proven right
p: Greek dikaiōthēsetai: when all is weighed, the Lord alone will stand in the right.
b: The verb is "justify" again (compare 13:22), here in the sense the Plain uses when God is the subject: "will be proven right." A psalm says to God, "So you are in the right when you speak" (Psalm 51:4), and Paul quotes the Greek of that psalm: "So that you may be proved right in your words" (Romans 3:4). Ben Sira's one-line verse, with the even shorter 18:1, opens a hymn on God's greatness and human smallness (18:1-14).

a: who will track down all his great deeds?
t: No one can search out his works
p: A theme of the psalms and of Paul: God's greatness cannot be fully told or traced.
b: "There is no searching out his greatness" (Psalm 145:3); "Will you get to the bottom of God by searching?" (Job 11:7). Paul ends his long argument in Romans with the same wonder: "No one can search out his judgments or follow the tracks of his ways!" (Romans 11:33). The Greek exichniazō, "track down, trace the footprints," is a hunter's word; Ben Sira used its root for the seeker of Wisdom as a "tracker" (14:22).

a: There is no taking away and no adding
t: Nothing to add, nothing to take away
p: Ecclesiastes says the same of God's works, in the same pair of verbs.
b: "I know that all that God does will be forever. There is no adding to it and no taking away from it" (Ecclesiastes 3:14). Moses used the pair of the Law itself (Deuteronomy 4:2), and Revelation of its own words (Revelation 22:18-19). For Ben Sira, God's wonders are complete; human beings cannot improve them, and cannot even trace them to the end.

a: A person comes to the end and finds he is only starting
p: However far a person searches into God's works, he finds he has only begun, as Ecclesiastes says.
b: "He has also put forever in their hearts, yet no human can find out the work God has done, from the beginning to the end" (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Ben Sira puts it as a paradox: when a man finishes, he is at the start; when he stops, he is at a loss. Isaiah says the same of God's understanding: "There is no getting to the bottom of his understanding" (Isaiah 40:28).

a: What is a human being, and what is he worth?
p: The question of Psalm 8, Psalm 144 and Job, asked here to show how small we are next to God.
b: "LORD, what is a human being, that you know him, / a son of man, that you keep him in mind?" (Psalm 144:3; compare Psalm 8:4). In Psalm 8 the question leads to wonder at the honor God gives humans; in Job 7:17 to complaint. Ben Sira uses it for humility: next to the eternal God, a human life is a drop in the sea (18:10). Yet the answer he goes on to give is God's patience and mercy (18:11-14).

a: a hundred years
p: Ben Sira counts a long life as a hundred years; the psalm says seventy or eighty.
b: The psalm says, "The days of our years add up to seventy, / or eighty for the strong" (Psalm 90:10). Genesis gives 120 years as the limit after the flood (Genesis 6:3), and Isaiah's new Jerusalem counts dying at a hundred as dying young (Isaiah 65:20). Ben Sira's "a hundred years, if they are many" is the long life a person might hope for. The longer Greek adds a line about the sleep of death that awaits everyone.

a: within the day of eternity
p: A life is to eternity as a drop is to the sea. The longer Greek says "a thousand years," as in Psalm 90 and 2 Peter.
b: "For a thousand years, as you see them, / are like yesterday after it has gone by" (Psalm 90:4). 2 Peter repeats it: "in the Lord's sight one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years like one day" (2 Peter 3:8). Vaticanus says "a few years" are as nothing beside "the day of eternity"; the longer Greek, followed by the KJV, says "a thousand years" (see the variant). Both make the same point, and both lead straight to God's patience (18:11).

a: So the Lord bears with them a long time
p: Because human life is so short and weak, God is patient: the reasoning of 2 Peter and Romans as well.
b: The Greek makrothymeō is "to be long-tempered," slow to anger, the quality God names at Sinai (Exodus 34:6, "slow to anger"). 2 Peter says, "he bears patiently with you. He does not want any to be lost, but wants all to arrive at repentance" (2 Peter 3:9), and Paul asks, "do you make light of the riches of his kindness, his forbearance and his patience?" (Romans 2:4). Ben Sira gives the reason from the human side: God knows how short and frail our lives are (18:9-12), as the psalm says, "he keeps in mind that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14).

a: but the Lord's mercy reaches all flesh
p: God's mercy reaches every living being, not only Israel, and he leads like a shepherd.
b: Human mercy reaches a neighbor; God's reaches "all flesh." Jonah learns the same: "should I not have pity on Nineveh, the great city ... and many animals too?" (Jonah 4:11), and Wisdom of Solomon says, "you show mercy to all" (Wisdom of Solomon 11:23). The shepherd who corrects and brings back his flock is the God of Isaiah 40:11, "Like a shepherd he will graze his flock," and of Ezekiel 34, who seeks the lost and brings back the stray (Ezekiel 34:16); Jesus calls himself "the good shepherd" (John 10:11). Here Ben Sira agrees fully with the 66 books.
r: Jonah 4:11; Wisdom of Solomon 11:23; Isaiah 40:11; Ezekiel 34:16; John 10:11; Luke 15:4-7

a: those who welcome discipline
p: God's correction is a sign of his love, as Proverbs and Hebrews say.
b: Here paideia is God's correction, so the Plain says "discipline" (see 16:25). "The LORD's discipline, my son, do not reject ... For whoever the LORD loves, he rebukes" (Proverbs 3:11-12), quoted in Hebrews: "For whoever the Lord loves, he disciplines" (Hebrews 12:6). Ben Sira joins it to mercy: God has mercy on those who accept his correction and hurry to his judgments.

a: do not let any gift come with words that hurt
p: A gift spoiled by scolding loses its good. Paul and James say God gives freely, and loves a glad giver.
b: Ben Sira turns to how to give (18:15-18): do not stain a good deed with blame, or a gift with hurtful words; a kind word can do more than a present. "God loves a glad giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7), and God himself "gives to everyone with an open hand and without scolding" (James 1:5). Jesus' warning not to give alms to be seen (Matthew 6:2-4) is about the giver's heart, as this is.

a: a gracious man
p: The Greek kecharitōmenos is the participle the angel uses of Mary in Luke 1:28.
b: "A gracious man" is anēr kecharitōmenos, "a man who has been graced." The same participle, feminine, is the angel's greeting to Mary: kecharitōmenē, "you who have been shown favor" (Luke 1:28), the word the Latin tradition renders "full of grace." Paul uses the verb once, of God's grace "which he freely gave us" (Ephesians 1:6). Here the word describes a person whose words and gifts are both full of kindness. In Sirach the word is not a doctrine but a description of a generous man.

a: see to your health before sickness comes
p: Learn before speaking and care for your health before illness: Ben Sira later praises the physician (38:1-15).
b: "Giving a reply before you have heard / is foolish of you and a disgrace" (Proverbs 18:13), and James says, "let every person be ready to listen, slow to talk" (James 1:19). The second line uses therapeuou, "take care of yourself, get treatment," a word for medical care. Ben Sira values doctors and medicine (38:1-15). This line and the next are a series of "before" sayings: prepare before judgment, humble yourself before sickness, prepare before a vow (18:20-23).

a: Look into yourself ahead of the judgment
p: Paul gives the same advice: if we judged ourselves, we would not come under judgment.
b: "But if we judged ourselves, we would not come under judgment" (1 Corinthians 11:31; compare 2 Corinthians 13:5; Lamentations 3:40). The "hour of visitation" (Greek episkopē) is the time God comes to inspect and judge, whether in a crisis of this life or at death (18:24). Ben Sira promises that those who examine themselves will then find "forgiveness" (exilasmos; see the note on 16:7).

a: do not wait until death to be justified
p: Here "justified" means cleared of a debt such as an unpaid vow before death, not Paul's doctrine of justification.
b: The Greek dikaiōthēnai, "to be justified," here means to be set right or cleared, as one settles a debt. The debt in view is the unpaid vow of the first line: "When you make a vow to the LORD your God, do not be slow to pay it" (Deuteronomy 23:21; compare Ecclesiastes 5:4-5). The Latin reads quite differently: "Let nothing hinder thee from praying always, and be not afraid to be justified even to death: for the reward of God continueth for ever" (Douay) (see the variant).

a: do not act like a man who puts the Lord to the test
p: A rash vow tests God, as Israel did at Massah. Jesus quotes the same command.
b: "Do not put the LORD your God to the test, the way you tested him at Massah" (Deuteronomy 6:16), the verse Jesus quotes to the tempter (Matthew 4:7). A vow made without thought, then left unpaid, treats God as if he did not care. The Greek euxasthai can mean either "pray" or "make a vow," and the KJV has "Before thou prayest"; the Plain says "make a vow" because 18:22 is about vows, and a corrector of Sinaiticus makes the vow itself the thing to prepare (see the variant).

a: when he turns his face away
p: God turning away his face is the Bible's picture of judgment and abandonment.
b: "I will abandon them and hide my face from them" (Deuteronomy 31:17); "How long will your face stay hidden from me?" (Psalm 13:1). The "end of your days" (Greek teleutē, "death") is when Ben Sira expects God's anger to fall on the unrepentant; he says nothing here about a judgment after death.

a: Remember the season of famine while you have your fill
p: Plan for hunger in years of plenty, as Joseph did in Egypt.
b: Joseph stored grain in the seven good years so that it would be "a reserve for the land for the seven years of famine" (Genesis 41:36). Ben Sira turns it into personal advice: in good times remember how quickly things change, for "between dawn and dusk the season turns" (18:26). Proverbs prays for neither poverty nor riches (Proverbs 30:8-9).

a: Do not walk behind your desires
p: Vaticanus writes a title, "Self-control of the soul," at the start of this verse; the Plain's heading translates it.
b: The Greek manuscripts of Sirach have section titles, and Codex Vaticanus writes Enkrateia psychēs, "Self-control of the soul," at the head of 18:30. Swete's notes say Sinaiticus puts the same title before 18:15. The Plain's heading "Self-Control" translates it. Enkrateia is the last item in Paul's fruit of the Spirit, "gentleness, self-control" (Galatians 5:23), and the athlete's discipline: "Everyone who competes controls himself in everything" (1 Corinthians 9:25). Ben Sira's section (18:30-19:3) is about appetite, luxury and debt.

a: throwing in for banquets with loans
t: Paying your share of the feast
p: Greek symbolokopeō is to spend on shared feasts; the Septuagint uses it for the "glutton" son of Deuteronomy 21:20.
b: In Greek cities friends held dinners where each guest paid a share, the symbolē (18:32). Ben Sira warns the young man not to keep up with such company on borrowed money. The verb symbolokopeō, "to spend on feasts," appears in the Septuagint of Deuteronomy 21:20, where the parents say of their rebellious son, "He is a glutton and a drunkard" (Greek symbolokopōn oinophlygei). The Hebrew of 18:33 in Cairo Genizah manuscript C (folio V recto, line 3) uses the same Hebrew pair as Deuteronomy, "do not be a glutton and a drunkard," and Proverbs warns that "the drunkard and the glutton lose everything they have" (Proverbs 23:21).
orig: συμβολοκοπῶν ἐκ δανισμοῦ; Hebrew אל תהי זולל וסובא
